## Introduction
We have learned that we can find the eigenvalues of a matrix by finding the roots of the characteristic polynomial, 
but finding the roots of a high degree polynomial can be difficult in itself!
It turns out that this problem can be turned up side down: We can in fact use linear algebra to find the roots of the characteristic polynomial. 
In fact, most software find eigenvalues by following this approach, rather than finding them directly as roots in a polynomial!
We shall look at this linear algebra procedure, which can be viewed as a general method for finding roots in polynomials numerically. 
Given the polynomial 
$$ p(t)=a_0+a_1t+\cdots + a_{n-1}t^{n-1}+t^n,$$
we define the companion matrix $C(p)$ by
$$
C(p)
=
\left(\begin{array}{rrrrr} 
  0 & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 
  0 & 0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\ 
  \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ 
  0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 1 \\ 
  -a_0 & -a_1 & -a_2 & \cdots & -a_{n-1} 
\end{array}\right).
$$

::: {#exr-1}
(a) Show that the characteristic polynomial of $C(p)$ is given by $\det(C(p)-\lambda I)=(-1)^n p(\lambda)$, 
so that the eigenvalues of $C(p)$ correspond to the roots of $p$. 

::::: {.callout-tip title='Hint' collapse="true"}
Expand the determinant along the last row.
:::::

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
We have 
$$
C(p) - \lambda I
=
\left(\begin{array}{rrrrr} 
  -\lambda & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 
  0 & -\lambda & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\ 
  \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ 
  0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 1 \\ 
  -a_0 & -a_1 & -a_2 & \cdots & -a_{n-1} - \lambda I
\end{array}\right).
$$
When expanding the determinant along the last row we get the minors 
$$1,-\lambda,\lambda^2,...,(-1)^{n-1}\lambda^{n-1},$$
so that the determinant is
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\sum_{k=1}^{n-1} (-1)^{n+k+1}a_{k-1} (-1)^{k-1}\lambda^{k-1}      +      (-1)^{2n+1}(a_{n-1}+\lambda) (-1)^{n-1}\lambda^{n-1} \\
&= (-1)^n \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} a_{k-1} \lambda^{k-1}    +   (-1)^n\lambda^n (a_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1} +\lambda^n)  \\
&= (-1)^n \sum_{k=1}^n a_{k-1} \lambda^{k-1} + (-1)^n\lambda^n \\
&= (-1)^n p(\lambda).
\end{aligned}
$$
:::::::
:::::

(b) Show that $C(p)$ is invertible if and only if $a_0\neq 0$, and that 
$$
  C(p)^{-1} 
  = 
  \left(\begin{array}{rrrrr}  
    -\frac{a_1}{a_0} & -\frac{a_2}{a_0} & \cdots & -\frac{a_{n-1}}{a_0} & -\frac{1}{a_0}\\ 
    1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ 
    0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ 
    \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ 
    0 & 0 & \cdots & 1 & 0 
  \end{array}\right).
$$

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
A matrix is invertible if and only if $\lambda=0$ is not an eigenvalue, and $\lambda=0$ is a root in $(-1)^n p(\lambda)$ if and only if $a_0=0$. 
For the second part we compute
$$
\left(\begin{array}{rrrrr} 
  0 & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 
  0 & 0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\ 
  \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ 
  0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 1 \\ 
  -a_0 & -a_1 & -a_2 & \cdots & -a_{n-1} 
\end{array}\right)
\left(\begin{array}{rrrrr}  
    -\frac{a_1}{a_0} & -\frac{a_2}{a_0} & \cdots & -\frac{a_{n-1}}{a_0} & -\frac{1}{a_0}\\ 
    1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ 
    0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ 
    \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ 
    0 & 0 & \cdots & 1 & 0 
  \end{array}\right)$$
component by component.
:::::::
:::::
:::

::: {#exr-2}
Suppose that $\lambda$ is a root in $p(t)$, in other words an eigenvalue for $C(p)$ according to Exercise 1. 
Show that $(1,\lambda,\lambda^2,...,\lambda^{n-1})$ is a corresponding eigenvector for $C(p)$.

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
We have that
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\left(\begin{array}{rrrrr} 
  0 & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 
  0 & 0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\ 
  \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ 
  0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 1 \\ 
  -a_0 & -a_1 & -a_2 & \cdots & -a_{n-1} 
\end{array}\right)
\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ \lambda \\ \lambda^2 \\ \vdots \\ \lambda^{n-1} \end{pmatrix} \\
&= \begin{pmatrix} \lambda \\ \lambda^2 \\ \vdots \\ \lambda^{n-1} \\ -a_0-a_1\lambda-a_2\lambda^2 - \cdots - a_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1} \end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix} \lambda \\ \lambda^2 \\ \vdots \\ \lambda^{n-1} \\ \lambda^n-p(\lambda) \end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix} \lambda \\ \lambda^2 \\ \vdots \\ \lambda^{n-1} \\ \lambda^n \end{pmatrix} \\
&= \lambda \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ \lambda \\ \lambda^2 \\ \vdots \\ \lambda^{n-1} \end{pmatrix} 
\end{aligned}
$$
:::::::
:::::
:::

In the following we shall let $\lambda_1,...,\lambda_n$ be the roots in $p(t)$, repeated with multiplicity. Define the Vandermonde matrix 
$$\mathbf{V} = \left(\begin{array}{rrrr} 1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 \\ \lambda_1 & \lambda_2 & \cdots & \lambda_n \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ \lambda_1^{n-1} & \lambda_2^{n-1} & \cdots & \lambda_n^{n-1} \end{array} \right).$$
It is clear that $V$ is not invertible when a $\lambda_i$ has multiplicity larger than $1$, since two columns in $V$ then are equal. 
$V$ is invertible when the $\lambda_1,\ldots\lambda_n$ are distinct, since eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent - 
this implies that the columns in $V$ provide a basis. 
It follows that $V$ is invertible if and only if all $\lambda_1,...,\lambda_n$ are distinct.
Let $D$ be the diagonal matrix with $\lambda_1,...,\lambda_n$ on the diagonal. We then have that
$$ C(p)=VDV^{-1},$$
so that $C(p)$ is diagionalisable, with $V$ diagonalising it.

We can also define the companion matrix $C(A)$ of a matrix $A$ to be the companion matrix of $(-1)^n$ times the characteristic polynomial of $A$.

$C(A)$ and $A$ have the same eigenvalues, since they by definition have the same characteristic polynomial. 
Aided by Exercise 3, $C(A)$ can be constructed without actually knowing the eigenvalues. 
Since $C(A)$ has a simpler form (most elements in the matrix are $0$), it is easier computationally to compute powers of this matrix.  
This makes it computationally easier to use the power method (and other methods!), which enables us to find the unknown eigenvalues.

With the power method we only found approximations to the biggest eigenvalue above. 
The *QR-method* is a method for finding eigenvalues which is very similar to Jacobi's method. In particular it can be used to find approximations to 
all eigenvalues. 
Again we start with a symmetric matrix $A$, and apply similarity transformations (so that all matrices have the same eigenvalues), 
In Jacobi's method the similarity transformations were plane rotations. In the QR-method they are given by the QR-factorisation: 

::: {#exr-45}
Let $A=QR$ be a $QR$-factorisation of $A$. Show that the matrices $QR$ and $RQ$ are similar.

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
We have that $Q(RQ)Q^{-1} = QR$. Since $Q$ is orthogonal it follows that $QR$ and $RQ$ are similar. 
:::::::
:::::
:::

It follows that $QR$ and RQ$ have the same eigenvalues. 
If $A_k=Q_kR_k$ is a QR-factorisation of $A_k$, we set $A_{k+1}=Q_k^TA_kQ_k$. 
We now get $A_{k+1}=Q_k^TQ_kR_kQ^k=R_kQ_k$. 
We will test this on the same matrix $A$ as before.




We define $A_1=RQ=Q_1R_1$ (where $Q_1R_1$ is the $QR$-factorisation of $A_1$), 
and then $A_2=R_1Q_1=Q_2R_2$ (where $Q_2R_2$ is the $QR$-factorisation of $A_2$), and so on, 
we get a sequence of matrices $A,A_1,A_2,\ldots$, which all have the same eigenvalues.
